title: Who am I here?
hookLine: remember who you are, a human, a citizen, a son, a brother, and act from each (Discourses 2.10)
carry: each name tells you what to do

lines: THE WRONG ONE IN THE ROOM.
cards: In a single afternoon you might be a manager in a meeting, a customer on hold, a daughter on the phone with her mother, a neighbor waving across the fence, and a stranger letting someone merge in traffic.

Each one asks something slightly different of you. It's easy to switch without noticing, and sometimes to bring the wrong one into the room: the boss into the family dinner, the tired customer into a talk with a friend.
Epictetus had a method for this.

teach.b: This is Discourses book two, chapter ten: how to find what you owe from the names you carry. Consider who you are, Epictetus says.
First, a human being, which means someone with a will, and nothing in you ranks higher than that.

Second, a citizen of the world, a part of it, and not a minor part. So act the way a hand or a foot would act if it could think: never just for itself, always as part of the whole body. Then the names come closer to home.
Remember you're a son. That name asks you to treat what's yours as your father's, to give way to him, never to speak badly of him to others.
Remember you're a brother: yield, be courteous, and never fight your brother over things that don't really matter. If you sit on a city council, remember you're a councilor.
If young, young; if old, old; if a father, a father.

teach.h: EACH NAME TELLS YOU WHAT TO DO.
teach.b: Each name, if you stop and think about it, tells you what to do.
His examples are sons, brothers and fathers. The method fits daughters, sisters, parents, partners, coworkers, anyone.
And it's simple enough to use at a doorway: which name am I carrying into this room, and what does it ask of me?

how: Some Stoic readers pause before entering a room or conversation to name the role they're stepping into, and ask what it asks of them.

o: a nickname a teacher gives to a student
name: each role you carry, and what it asks of you

s: Epictetus starts with your job title
he starts with being a human being, then a citizen of the world.
he says a citizen of the world acts like a hand or foot that could think
never just for itself, always as part of the whole.
the method only fits sons and brothers

games.q: you're about to walk into a room and you're not sure how to act. what does Epictetus say to do?
o: ask which name you carry here, and what it asks of you.
games.why: he says each name, human, citizen, son, brother, councilor, father, tells you what to do if you think about it.

practice: Think of the next place you'll walk into today, an office, a kitchen, a classroom, a call, and name who you'll be there: parent, colleague, friend, neighbor.
Ask what that name asks of you, patience, honesty, generosity, and let one quality come forward. Picture crossing the doorway carrying it.

wordCard.voice: Onoma. Greek for name: Epictetus' method of names, human, citizen of the world, child, sibling, parent, each telling you what you owe.

orig.note: Greek onoma: a name; Epictetus says the names we carry show us our duties.
